sections.title: Listening. Listen to an interview with a young film-maker. Are the sentences true or false?
sections.script:
Host: Today I'm talking to Sevara, who is only seventeen but has already made three short films. Sevara, how did you start?
Sevara: I started with my phone when I was thirteen. I made funny videos about my cat. My friends loved them, so I tried to tell real stories.
Host: What is your new film about?
Sevara: It's about a grandmother who teaches her grandson to cook. It's quite emotional — some people cry at the end!
Host: Was it expensive to make?
Sevara: Not at all. We didn't have much money, so my family were the actors and we filmed everything in our kitchen.
Host: What's the hardest part of making a film?
Sevara: Editing. It takes much longer than filming. For a ten-minute film, I spent about forty hours on the computer.
Host: And what's next?
Sevara: A film festival in Tashkent has chosen my film, so I'm going there next month. I'm really nervous!

sections.title: H. Read the text and choose the correct answers.
sections.passage:
Have you ever wanted to be in a film? Every year, film companies need hundreds of ‘extras’ — the people you see walking in the street or sitting in a café behind the main actors.

You don’t need acting experience, but you do need patience. A day on a film set can last twelve hours, and you might spend ten of them waiting. Experienced extras always take a book or some music. Directors prefer people who are calm and follow instructions; if you complain or are late, they won’t call you again.

The pay is not high — about the same as working in a shop — and you will probably never see your face clearly on screen. So why do people do it? Many say it’s the experience: you see how films are made, you meet interesting people and, sometimes, you stand two metres from a star.
